prompt.context: The Carolina Symphony Orchestra (CSO) is in trouble. Despite recently doubling down on marketing and advertising, the orchestra's profitability has consistently dropped for the last several years. The executive board has enlisted your help to diagnose the cause of this nosedive and reverse it. The CSO must find a sustainable method to generate net-new profits over the next two years to hit its strategic growth goals.
prompt.question: What is driving the CSO's profitability decline, and what recommendation would you make to generate an incremental $3M in profit over the next two years?

clarifying_info.a: The CSO is the only professional symphony in the area, but it competes with other high-caliber entertainment providers. It plays mainly classical music but does incorporate some popular music.

clarifying_info.q: What products or offerings does the CSO provide?
clarifying_info.a: The CSO provides a range of offerings including group, single, and subscription tickets, in addition to community education and engagement events and public concerts.
Revenue is split into three categories: earned (ticket and concession sales), contributed (donations and grants), and investment (securities).
The main segment consists of older, wealthier consumers, although there is a burgeoning interest in the orchestra among younger subscribers.

clarifying_info.q: What is the specific profit target?
clarifying_info.a: The overall goal is incremental profit of $3M over the next two years.

exhibits.title: Carolina Symphony Orchestra: Revenue & Cost (2017-2019)
exhibits.shows: A grouped bar chart showing annual totals (in $M) for Costs, Contributed Revenue, Earned Revenue, and Investment Revenue for years 2017, 2018, and 2019
exhibits.data: Bars for each of the four categories across three years; Costs appear relatively stable around $10-11M; Earned Revenue shows the most visible decline; Contributed Revenue and Investment Revenue also shown with smaller changes

exhibits.title: Ticket Sales Data (2017-2019)
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down ticket sales by category (Single Attendance, Premium Subscription, Group) showing number of tickets sold and average ticket price for each year 2017-2019

exhibits.title: Subscriber Preferences by Segment
exhibits.shows: A Harvey ball matrix showing how much each subscriber segment (5+ Years 31%, 1-5 Years 18%, <1 Year 51%) values six characteristics: Musical Selection, # of Concerts per Season, Quality of Guest Artists, Quality of Orchestra, Programming Variety, Quality of Venue; also includes a pie chart of 2019-2020 Subscriber Distribution by tenure
exhibits.data: Subscriber Distribution: <1 Year 51%, 5+ Years 31%, 1-5 Years 18% | Harvey balls indicate varying levels of importance per characteristic per segment (full, three-quarter, half, quarter circles)

exhibits.title: Improving Orchestra Quality: Options
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of two options for improving orchestra quality: Option 1 Hire Renowned Conductor and Option 2 Increase Principal Chair Salaries, with annual cost and expected revenue for Year 1 and Year 2
exhibits.data: Option 1 (Conductor): Cost/Year $1.5M, Expected Revenue Yr1 $3.0M, Yr2 $3.5M | Option 2 (Principal Chair Salaries): Cost/Year $0.5M, Expected Revenue Yr1 $2.0M, Yr2 $2.5M

framework: Revenue Benchmarking: Break down revenue by type — Earned (ticket volume x price by ticket type), Contributed (donation size and frequency), Investment (portfolio composition and returns)
Cost Benchmarking: Identify Fixed costs (facilities, performer salaries, insurance) vs. Variable costs (printed materials, concessions, booking fees); check for cost creep
Customer Profiling: Understand distribution of ticket holders by age, income, and visit frequency; assess brand awareness and product attractiveness
Competitive Analysis: Estimate CSO's share of local live entertainment market; benchmark ticket prices vs. comparable entertainment; compare industry best practices to current strategy

questions.prompt: After reviewing Exhibit 1a, what is the primary driver of the profitability decline — costs or revenues? Which revenue stream is most responsible?
questions.guidance: The candidate should quickly observe that costs are relatively stable (operating costs move only slightly year-over-year from ~$10.6M to ~$11.2M), ruling out a cost problem. The main driver is a sharp decline in Earned Revenue. Investment Revenue also declines but more slowly and with less total impact. Contributed Revenue shows modest change. The candidate should conclude this is primarily an earned-revenue (ticket sales) problem and ask for a more granular breakdown.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1b, calculate the revenue for each ticket category in each year and identify which segment is the primary driver of the earned revenue decline.
questions.guidance: Candidates should multiply tickets sold by average price for each category and year. Group tickets are essentially flat and can be eliminated as a driver. Both Single Attendance and Premium Subscription are declining, but the candidate must compute total dollar impact, not just compare ticket volumes. Premium Subscription is the largest revenue-generating segment and shows the biggest total dollar decline ($1.14M over the period), making it the primary driver. The simultaneous drop in both price and volume for subscriptions is notable — this could indicate adverse price signaling or that management is cutting prices reactively without addressing root causes.

math.setup: Revenue = # Tickets Sold x Avg. Ticket Price for each category and year
math.answer: Premium Subscription revenue declined by $1.14M total (2017 to 2019), making it the single largest driver. Single Attendance fell $0.14M. Group is flat/negligible.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2a, which subscriber preference characteristic should the CSO prioritize to retain and grow subscription revenue?
questions.guidance: Good candidates focus on 'Quality of Guest Artists' and 'Quality of Orchestra' as the two most filled Harvey balls. Excellent candidates go further and calculate a weighted score for each characteristic using the subscriber segment distribution (5+ Yrs = 31%, 1-5 Yrs = 18%, <1 Yr = 51%) and the Harvey ball fill levels (full=1, three-quarter=0.75, half=0.5, quarter=0.25). Quality of Orchestra scores higher than Quality of Guest Artists when weighted properly, making it the mathematically most valued characteristic. Candidates should note that new subscribers (<1 year, 51% of base) drive this result.

math.setup: Weighted score = (Harvey ball fill for 5+ Yrs x 0.31) + (Harvey ball fill for 1-5 Yrs x 0.18) + (Harvey ball fill for <1 Yr x 0.51). Harvey ball readings from exhibit: Guest Artists — 5+Yrs full (1), 1-5Yrs half (0.5), <1Yr half (0.5). Orchestra — 5+Yrs full (1), 1-5Yrs quarter (0.25), <1Yr three-quarter (0.75).
math.answer: Quality of Orchestra scores 73.75 vs. Quality of Guest Artists at 65.5 — Orchestra Quality is the more impactful lever to prioritize.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2b and an interest rate of 10%, calculate the NPV of each option and determine whether either option meets the $3M profit threshold over two years.
questions.guidance: Candidates should recognize that NPV = (Net Cash Flow Yr1)/(1.1) + (Net Cash Flow Yr2)/(1.21). Net cash flow = Expected Revenue minus Cost per year. Strong candidates notice both options have identical net cash flows ($1.5M in Yr1, $2.0M in Yr2) and therefore equivalent NPVs — only one NPV calculation is needed. Both options narrowly exceed the $3M threshold (~$3.02M). Excellent candidates identify this mathematical equivalence and then use qualitative reasoning to differentiate between options.

math.setup: Net Cash Flow = Expected Revenue - Annual Cost; NPV = NCF_Yr1 / 1.10 + NCF_Yr2 / 1.21
steps: Both options yield NPV of approximately $3.02M, which meets the $3M target.
math.answer: Both options have NPV ~$3.02M; they are mathematically equivalent. The choice must be made on qualitative grounds.

brainstorming.prompt: The board agrees that the subscription ticket holder category is mainly to blame for the eroding bottom line. Based on this trend, what are some levers that the board could pull to boost the revenue generated by its subscription-holding patrons?

categories.name: Understand Consumer Base
ideas: Profile demographic of subscription holders (families, age range, income level)
Analyze purchasing patterns and what triggers lapsed subscribers to cancel

categories.name: Subscriber Research
ideas: Survey subscription holders to determine the most important aspects of purchasing behavior (e.g. programming quality, special guest artists)
Study what prompted <1 year subscribers to join and what may cause them to leave

categories.name: Targeted Marketing
ideas: Social media campaigns aimed at younger demographics and lapsed subscribers
Direct mail campaigns to recapture business of former subscription holders
Leverage burgeoning younger-audience interest to reposition brand

categories.name: Subscription Product Enhancement
ideas: Add or expand concert offerings per season
Include premium perks such as lounge access or soloist meet-and-greets
Bundle subscription with other experiences (education events, backstage tours)

categories.name: Pricing Strategy
ideas: Consider a price increase to reverse potential negative price signaling — decreasing prices may have signaled to customers an initial overvaluing of the product
Introduce tiered subscription tiers to capture different willingness-to-pay levels

recommendation: Both Option 1 (Hire Renowned Conductor) and Option 2 (Increase Principal Chair Salaries) generate equivalent NPVs of approximately $3.02M over two years, narrowly meeting the $3M threshold — so the financial case does not differentiate the two. The preferred recommendation depends on strategic priorities: Option 1 (Conductor) is better if the CSO needs immediate brand visibility and a high-profile name to attract new subscribers quickly; Option 2 (Principal Chair Salaries) is preferable if the CSO prioritizes long-term institutional stability and retention of its best musicians with more controllable cost structure.
Either option is defensible; the candidate should state a clear preference and tie it back to the $3M goal and the subscriber base finding from Exhibit 2a.
risks: Projected revenue figures for both options may be inaccurate — subscriber preferences vary significantly across segments, so actual uptake is uncertain
Option 1 (Conductor): search process is costly and time-consuming; the musical community may reject the orchestra's choice of conductor
Option 2 (Salaries): the orchestra may already have best-in-class principal chairs; raising one group's pay may create a domino effect on broader musician compensation
Both options only narrowly exceed the $3M NPV threshold, leaving little margin for underperformance
next_steps: Option 1 (Conductor): formally announce the search and engage an industry headhunter to lead a targeted national/international candidate search; benchmark candidate profiles against peer orchestras
Option 2 (Salaries): conduct an internal assessment of all principal chair salaries and review past audition and performance data to determine how increases should be distributed optimally
Both options: conduct internal benchmarking of projected revenue figures against comparable orchestras to validate assumptions; track subscriber retention metrics quarterly
